summary: Discusses how to build sensors and other devices that use the Constrained Application Protocol over cellular networks, focusing on keeping power use low. The memo covers techniques for minimizing power consumption in such devices. It is informational advice, not a new protocol.

eli5.summary: Tips for making a battery-powered gadget talk on a phone network while using as little battery as possible.

questions: how to reduce power use of coap devices
how to extend battery life of sensors
subtitle: Techniques for building battery-powered IoT devices that communicate over cellular networks.

tldr.problem: Battery-powered sensors and devices on cellular networks need to minimize energy use to achieve practical lifetimes of years or more, yet standard protocols are often optimized for throughput rather than power.
tldr.mechanism: The memo provides guidelines for using CoAP on 3GPP cellular networks (2G, 3G, LTE, 5G) to reduce power consumption, separating devices into two scenarios: real-time reachable devices that stay listening, and sleepy devices that wake only when needed.
tldr.outcome: By following the techniques in this memo, developers can minimize communication overhead and radio usage at the application and protocol layers, complementing hardware improvements and network evolution.

facts.label: CoAP implementation size
facts.value: About 1,000 lines of code above IP layer

today: RFC 9178 is an Informational memo published in May 2022. The techniques it describes for power optimization at the protocol layer remain relevant, though advances in radio technology and network design continue to evolve the underlying cellular networks.

sections.title: Building Power-Efficient IoT Devices
sections.content:
CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) is simple and efficient enough that a full implementation above the IP layer can fit in just a thousand lines of code, making it ideal for resource-constrained sensors. However, optimizing power consumption for devices on cellular networks like LTE and 5G remains challenging and requires careful design at multiple layers.

This memo focuses on techniques to minimize power consumption at the IP, transport, and application layers when using CoAP over cellular networks. The guidance complements hardware improvements and network evolution but focuses on what developers can control today with existing technology.
sections.eli5: CoAP is a simple protocol that doesn't take much code to use, but making it work well on a phone network while saving battery power is tricky, and this memo explains how to do it.

sections.title: Power-Saving Goals and Constraints
sections.content:
Battery lifetime requirements vary greatly. Devices connected to power-over-Ethernet or mains power can use basic optimization, while true battery-powered devices or those powered by energy harvesting must be strict about power usage. Some applications require battery lifetimes of years or even a decade or longer.

Cellular networks present specific challenges: they are public networks without application-specific configuration, they use point-to-point links (so multicast discovery doesn't work), and radio reception for checking messages often consumes more power than transmission itself. Periodic paging checks to see if messages are waiting can be a far bigger drain than the actual data transfers.
sections.eli5: Some devices plug in to power, but battery ones need to carefully control when they wake up and listen, because checking for messages can use more battery than actually sending them.

sections.title: Real-Time Reachable Devices
sections.content:
Some devices must be reachable at any instant with small latency, such as light bulbs or door locks. These devices act as CoAP servers, meaning they must listen actively for incoming requests. They have limited control over when they receive messages and cannot use sleep states to save power.

For these devices, the main power savings come from tuning the frequency of packet reception checks to match application needs. The memo notes that CoAP's Observe extension (for tracking value changes) can reduce polling but does not reduce the time the device needs to stay listening for new requests.

To act as a server on a public network, the device needs a public IP address, an IPv6 address, or to reside on a private network (using a special APN or VPN) to avoid unwanted traffic that drains power.
sections.eli5: A smart light bulb has to stay ready to hear a command at any time, so it can't sleep much. But it can check less often if it doesn't need super-fast responses.

sections.title: Sleepy Devices
sections.content:
Many sensors, such as temperature monitors or heating controllers, report slowly changing values and can sleep most of the time. These devices act only as CoAP clients, meaning they wake up on their own schedule, send data, and shut down all communication channels during sleep periods. Sleep intervals can range from minutes to days depending on the application and power constraints.

The advantage is dramatic: radio and network communication can be turned off completely during sleep, reducing power consumption significantly. The trade-off is that the device consumes some power and time to reattach to the network when it wakes up. Additionally, sleepy devices are less vulnerable to unwanted traffic because they listen only part of the time.

To support sleepy devices, the device should register itself with a resource directory or mirror server, then send periodic updates. The server or broker can hold data for the device during sleep periods.
sections.eli5: A temperature sensor can wake up once a day, send its reading, then sleep for 24 hours. This saves a ton of battery because the radio is off most of the time.

sections.title: Discovery, Registration, and Data Formats
sections.content:
On public networks without application-specific configuration, devices must register themselves to be discovered. The memo recommends using a resource directory following RFC 9176 or similar mechanisms. Since multicast discovery doesn't work on point-to-point cellular links, devices should know the directory's DNS name via manual configuration, hardwiring by the manufacturer, or a delegating manufacturer server that redirects to an enterprise.

Data format choices affect message size and thus energy use. The memo recommends using compact formats like CBOR or SenML instead of XML or JSON to minimize the bits transmitted. Smaller messages mean lower power consumption and faster transfer.

Hardware implementation challenges include managing sleep modes carefully (it is not always easy to shut down everything except a clock), handling radio module re-attachment costs, and coordinating between the CPU and network layer so the CPU does not stay powered waiting for paging signals that won't arrive.
sections.eli5: The device needs to find and tell a server it is ready, which works differently on phone networks than local networks. And sending data in a tight format takes less battery than using plain text.
